analysis.one_liner: Extends private mortgage insurance cancellation rights to high-risk mortgages and preserves stronger state consumer protections.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote, and it never attracted a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998, homeowners with private mortgage insurance can ask to cancel it once they build enough equity, and it cancels automatically at a set point. But the law carved out an exception for so-called high-risk loans, leaving those borrowers paying premiums indefinitely. This bill would erase that exception and also stop the federal law from overriding state rules that give homeowners stronger cancellation rights. The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners with high-risk mortgages who pay private mortgage insurance every month. Under existing law they were excluded from the right to ask for cancellation and from automatic cancellation once their loan balance dropped. They would gain the same rights as other borrowers, plus any stronger protections their state law already provided.

how_it_helps.text: The Homeowners Protection Act of 1998 let borrowers request cancellation of private mortgage insurance and required automatic cancellation, but exempted high-risk loans from these protections; this bill strikes that exemption so high-risk borrowers get the same rights [S2][S3].

The bill rewrites the federal law's preemption clause so it does not override state laws that cancel mortgage insurance earlier, require more disclosure, or otherwise give borrowers greater protection [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private mortgage insurance companies, which would lose the premium income from high-risk loans once borrowers could cancel coverage. Lenders, who rely on that insurance to protect them when borrowers put little money down, could face stricter requirements from state laws that would now stand.

drawbacks.text: High-risk loans are priced that way because the borrower is more likely to default, and the insurance on them is more expensive to provide; forcing cancellation of that coverage could lead insurers to charge more for it or refuse to cover such loans, raising costs or reducing credit access for the very borrowers the bill aims to help.

The bill would amend the Homeowners Protection Act before its protections had even taken effect, forcing insurers, lenders, and servicers to adjust to new rules on top of a law passed just months earlier.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers affected, the benefit is direct: relief from insurance premiums they no longer need. The main honest cost is that insurers might price or restrict coverage on high-risk loans in response, and the bill's effect on credit availability for those borrowers is a real open question. On balance it is a targeted consumer-protection fix, not a sweeping change.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and its Housing subcommittee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce introduced the bill on August 6, 1998, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services [S1][S5].
The committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity, where it sat with no further action [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4], and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 without the bill advancing [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private mortgage insurers keep collecting premiums on high-risk loans without cancellation rights, and high-risk borrowers keep paying. Consumers gained nothing from this bill's death.

for.name: Rep. John J. LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Housing subcommittee and never took it up for a hearing or vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic-sponsored measure with zero cosponsors from either party, so no bipartisan or partisan split ever formed around it.

industries.note: These insurers profit from monthly premiums borrowers pay on low-down-payment loans. The bill would have extended cancellation rights to high-risk loans, cutting off premium income the current law lets them keep from those borrowers indefinitely.

Lenders rely on mortgage insurance to protect them on low-down-payment loans, and the bill would let some of that coverage be canceled earlier. At the same time, it would let stronger state disclosure and cancellation rules apply to their dealings with borrowers.
